title: Bluetooth Flaw in Dealer-Installed Car Alarms Puts 2.2 Million Vehicles at Risk
excerpt: UC San Diego researchers found that KARR and SWDS aftermarket security systems all share a single Bluetooth key, letting anyone within five yards unlock doors or disable ignitions.
body:
• UC San Diego researchers discovered that 2.2 million vehicles fitted with KARR or SWDS aftermarket security devices all share an identical Bluetooth authentication key, making every one of them vulnerable to remote unlock attacks from within five yards.
  • Affected cars were primarily sold through Honda, Toyota, Mazda, Ford, and Jeep dealerships in Southern California since 2017, though resales have spread vulnerable vehicles across the U.S., Canada, and Japan.
  • The devices remain active even when buyers decline the paid KARR subscription, and removing them requires disassembling the dashboard.
  • Manufacturer Acrisure released a firmware patch on July 20, 2026; vehicle owners can apply it through the KARR app.

An aftermarket car alarm system installed by more than 3,000 dealerships nationwide contains a critical Bluetooth vulnerability that could let a nearby attacker unlock doors, disable ignitions, and defeat the very anti-theft protections the device was designed to provide, according to research published this week by the University of California San Diego.

The flaw affects KARR and SWDS security modules manufactured by Acrisure Protection Group. Researchers found that every single unit ships with the same hardcoded Bluetooth authentication key—a design choice one researcher compared to "setting all passwords for a line of devices to 1234 and making it impossible to change the password."

How the Attack Works

The KARR device sits beneath the driver-side dashboard, wired into the vehicle's ignition and computer systems. It connects to a companion smartphone app over Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE), offering key-fob-style controls: locking and unlocking doors, honking the horn, flashing headlights, and immobilizing the engine.

https://x.com/FoxUSNews/status/2083165539581710564

Because every device uses the same static key, the UC San Diego team built a proof-of-concept Android app that impersonated the legitimate KARR software and transmitted unauthorized commands to nearby alarm units. Lead researcher Andrew demonstrated the ability to unlock vehicles, disable alarms, and prevent parked cars from starting—all from up to five yards away.

"Instead of smashing a window to get access to a vehicle, thieves could simply connect remotely via Bluetooth to the device inside the vehicle, and make it unlock car doors."

— Jerry Yu, co-author and UC San Diego computer science graduate

The flaw does not allow an attacker to start the engine or take control of a moving vehicle, limiting the threat to stationary targets. But once a car is unlocked, thieves can use locksmith-grade tools to start the engine and drive away.

2.2 Million Cars, Many Owners Unaware

Using WiGLE, a crowdsourced wireless-signal database, the researchers estimated that at least 2.2 million Bluetooth-enabled KARR units are deployed across the country. During a single 20-minute drive near the UC San Diego campus, they detected signals from 97 KARR-equipped vehicles using a standard Android phone.

Most affected cars were purchased from Honda, Toyota, Mazda, Ford, and Jeep dealerships in Southern California between 2017 and today. Secondhand resales have since scattered several hundred thousand vulnerable vehicles across the United States, into Canada, and as far as Japan.

A critical wrinkle: the device stays wired in and active even when a buyer declines the paid KARR subscription. It continues broadcasting Bluetooth signals while the engine runs and for up to 10 minutes afterward, creating both a security and a privacy risk. Historical WiGLE records could reveal a targeted vehicle's frequent locations over time.

"Removing the devices is not trivial. You have to open up the dashboard and cut and reconnect the wires that are deeply intertwined with the car's computers and ignition system."

— Yibo Wei, co-author and UC San Diego PhD candidate

Acrisure Responds With Patch

Acrisure released a firmware update on July 20, roughly 18 months after the researchers first disclosed the flaw. A company spokesperson characterized the attack as "highly complex" with "low risk under real-world conditions," and claimed only a small percentage of devices with certain Bluetooth components are actually affected—a figure at odds with the researchers' estimate.

Vehicle owners can install the patch through the KARR Security app, whether or not they have an active subscription. Cars with a "KARR" or "SWDS" sticker on the driver-side window are likely equipped with an affected device. For those unsure, checking beneath the bottom of the dashboard on the driver's side for a small button or module will confirm installation.

The researchers also notified the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration and disclosed vulnerabilities to all relevant manufacturers. They plan to present their full findings at the DEF CON conference in Las Vegas on August 9, 2026, and at the USENIX Security Symposium in Baltimore on August 12.

What to Watch For

The KARR episode underscores a growing concern in automotive cybersecurity: aftermarket hardware installed by dealerships often flies under the regulatory radar and may introduce attack surfaces that neither buyers nor regulators anticipated. A second manufacturer, Rockledge, makes similar devices that may also be vulnerable, though the researchers noted those are harder to attack and have not yet been validated. Anyone who purchased a car from a dealership in the past nine years—particularly in Southern California—should check for KARR hardware and apply the update without delay.
nri_angle: Indian-Americans who bought cars from affected Southern California dealerships—or purchased secondhand vehicles with KARR stickers—should check their dashboards and apply the firmware update immediately.
